partners.mechanism_chain: TP53 (HGNC:11998) —DISRUPTS→ Regulation of apoptosis (GO:0042981); Regulation of apoptosis (GO:0042981) —LEADS_TO→ Seizures (HP:0001250); TP53 (HGNC:11998) —DISRUPTS→ Cell cycle arrest (GO:0007049); Cell cycle arrest (GO:0007049) —LEADS_TO→ Hepatocellular carcinoma (MONDO:0007256). Loss-of-function mutations in TP53 disrupt its normal function in regulating apoptosis and cell cycle arrest. Disruption of apoptosis regulation can lead to neuronal hyperexcitability and seizures, characteristic of Unverricht-Lundborg syndrome. Concurrently, impaired cell cycle arrest in hepatocytes, due to TP53 dysfunction, promotes uncontrolled proliferation and ultimately leads to hepatocellular carcinoma.

partners.mechanism_chain: CSTB (HGNC:2549) —DISRUPTS→ autophagy-lysosome pathway (GO:0006915); autophagy-lysosome pathway (GO:0006915) —LEADS_TO→ progressive myoclonus epilepsy (HP:0001278); NCKAP1L (HGNC:30526) —DISRUPTS→ cytosolic protein deubiquitination (GO:0030902); cytosolic protein deubiquitination (GO:0030902) —LEADS_TO→ autoinflammation (HP:0011757); cytosolic protein deubiquitination (GO:0030902) —LEADS_TO→ immunodeficiency (HP:0011195). Mutations in CSTB impair the autophagy-lysosome pathway, leading to Unverricht-Lundborg syndrome. Mutations in NCKAP1L disrupt cytosolic protein deubiquitination, a process linked to both autoinflammation and immunodeficiency. raw.translational: Understanding the shared mechanistic link between CSTB and HBB could reveal novel therapeutic targets for both Unverricht-Lundborg syndrome and beta-thalassemia. For instance, interventions aimed at modulating neuronal excitability might have unforeseen benefits in beta-thalassemia patients with neurological complications, or vice versa.

partners.mechanism_chain: CSTB (HGNC:2513) —LEADS_TO→ Unverricht-Lundborg syndrome (MONDO:0009698); HBB (HGNC:4827) —DISRUPTS→ Hemoglobin synthesis (REACT:R-HSA-193928); Hemoglobin synthesis (REACT:R-HSA-193928) —LEADS_TO→ Dominant beta-thalassemia (MONDO:0011381). While Unverricht-Lundborg syndrome is primarily linked to CSTB mutations, and dominant beta-thalassemia to HBB mutations, this hypothesis posits a mechanistic overlap through the shared pathway of hemoglobin synthesis. Loss-of-function in HBB directly impairs this pathway, leading to beta-thalassemia. Although CSTB's role in Unverricht-Lundborg syndrome is more complex, involving its interaction with VGF and potential downstream effects on neuronal function, a hypothetical indirect link could emerge if severe disruptions in hemoglobin synthesis (as in beta-thalassemia) secondarily impact cellular processes that CSTB also regulates, or vice versa, if CSTB dysfunction indirectly affects erythropoiesis. This hypothesis converges on the shared pathway of hemoglobin synthesis as the point of overlap, with HBB being a direct component and CSTB having a potential indirect influence.
